title: Scam Emails
about: Spot the warning signs that give a scam email away.

cards.situation: Sam's phone buzzes. Your Bank says the account closes tomorrow.

image.alt: Sam stands beside a big phone lock screen showing 9:12 and one notification from Your Bank: URGENT: Your account will be closed in 24 hours.

cards.prompt: Sam opens the email. **Tap each line** to look closer.

parts.job: The name says Your Bank, but look after the @: yourbank-help.example. Your Bank's real address is yourbank.example.
URGENT, 24 hours! A hurry like this stops you thinking it through.
Your Bank knows your name. But names are easy to find, so a name never proves an email is real.
It wants your password and card number. Real companies never ask for those by email.
Press and hold a link to see where it goes. This one goes to yourbank-verify.example, not Your Bank.

cards.explanation: Five lines give this email away.

cards.prompt: Sam taps "Verify my account" and types the password. **Who gets it?**

image.alt: Sam has tapped Verify my account, which opened a sign-in page with a password typed in. Below, three choices: Your Bank's building; a laptop for yourbank-verify.example; a phone with a shield, Nobody: it's blocked.
image.revealAlt: The password flies as a key from the sign-in page to the yourbank-verify.example laptop, which now has it. Your Bank's building is untouched.

cards.explanation: The button really goes to yourbank-verify.example, so the password goes straight to them.

cards.title: Warning signs
cards.body: A **scam** email pretends to be someone you trust, and each clue that gives it away is a **warning sign**. Spot one? Skip its link and open the real app or website yourself.

image.alt: The same email with five amber tags: the sender @yourbank-help is a fake sender; URGENT, 24 hours is rushing you; Dear Customer has no name; asking for your password and card number asks for secrets; Verify my account is a fake link.

cards.prompt: Another "Your Bank" email. It's a scam. **Tap every warning sign.**
cards.explanation: All five: a fake sender, rushing you, no name, asking for secrets and a fake link.
cards.nudge: There are five. Go line by line and ask: would the real Your Bank do this?
cards.showAnswer: The sender, the subject, "Dear Valued Customer", the request for your PIN and the button. The time and sign-off are normal.

cards.prompt: Sam won a console but never entered. **Is "Claim my prize" safe?**

image.alt: An email from Prize Team, win@big-prizes.example. Subject: You WON a games console! Congratulations! Claim it within 1 hour. A big green Claim my prize button and a drawing of a games controller.
image.revealAlt: The claim page at big-prizes.example: Pay $4.99 postage to get your prize, with empty boxes for card number, expiry and CVC. A tag says: Too good to be true.

options.nudge: Forget how nice it sounds. Which warning signs from Sam's first email are here too?

options.text: No: it still rushes you to a link

options.nudge: Forget how nice it sounds. Which warning signs from Sam's first email are here too?

cards.explanation: A prize you never entered is too good to be true, and it still rushes you to a link.
cards.showAnswer: No: it rushes you (1 hour) to a link, for a competition Sam never entered. No entry means no real prize.

cards.prompt: An email uses Sam's real name and school: "Sign in today." **Tap what Sam should do.**

image.alt: An email from Your School, it@yourschool-accounts.example. Subject: Account deleted TODAY. Hi Sam, sign in today, or your school account is deleted. Below, three choices: tap Sign in; reply Is this real?; a school building, open the site yourself.

options.nudge: Does knowing Sam's name prove anything? And where would a tap really go?
Does knowing Sam's name prove anything? And where would a reply really go?

options.text: Open the school site yourself, or ask a teacher

cards.explanation: A name is easy to find, so it proves nothing: go to the school site yourself.
cards.showAnswer: Open the school site yourself, or ask a teacher. The link and the reply both go to whoever sent it.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
Scam emails (people call them **phishing**) pretend to be someone you trust; warning signs give them away.

**Try this:** On the next email you get, check the address after the @.

**Next:** A text says your parcel is stuck. It isn't.
